completed_log.date: 2026-09-14 (ebook generator recovery sprint, part 4 -- worker timeout / bounded generation)
items: The manuscript-QA/correction fix (v1.7.9) held. The owner then supplied a Render log revealing a different, more fundamental problem: a worker blocked in a network read, killed by Gunicorn's timeout handler (gunicorn/workers/base.py::handle_abort -> sys.exit(1) -> 'Worker exiting' -> a new worker booting), matching the customer symptom exactly (30% -> manuscript request runs -> worker dies/restarts -> 'We couldn't reach the Factory').

Classified this from the code path alone as Gunicorn's own SIGABRT timeout-kill mechanism -- a synchronous long-running-request architecture problem, not a manuscript-generation correctness problem -- without needing to see the literal 'WORKER TIMEOUT' log line.

Attempted to confirm the actual Gunicorn --timeout/worker count first, per the sprint's explicit requirement: grepped the entire repository and found zero Gunicorn configuration anywhere (no Procfile, not in requirements.txt) -- the real Start Command is Render-dashboard-only, outside this environment. Reported that gap honestly instead of guessing a number.

Chose the preferred, durable repair (Option B) over a timeout bump (Option A): services/ebook_project_workspace.py::execute_generate_manuscript and execute_correct_manuscript both gained a max_chapters_per_call bound, reusing run_chapter_pipeline's existing max_chapter_calls cap -- no new mechanism invented. When the bound stops chapter writing with nothing having actually failed, both functions now return early as IN_PROGRESS instead of running QA against a deliberately incomplete draft, with the same ledger/charge accounting replicated for the partial round and the stage's idempotency key deliberately left unmarked (so the next call continues rather than replaying the same partial result forever).

Wired services/ebook_build_orchestrator.py::_run_manuscript to pass MANUSCRIPT_CHAPTERS_PER_ADVANCE=1 to both calls and return immediately on IN_PROGRESS, never calling approve_stage against incomplete content -- each /advance call now writes or repairs at most one chapter, reusing the existing checkpoint/resume loop for the rest, exactly the contract every other build stage already follows.

Found and fixed the attempts-ceiling problem this change would otherwise have introduced: a real book needing ~10+ incremental /advance calls would have hit the global 3-attempt ceiling and failed after 3 chapters. Added a per-stage attempts-ceiling override (manuscript=60); every other stage's ceiling is unchanged.
Preserved the customer-facing 'Writing your chapters (N of M)' message during this loop instead of generic retry wording, via a small marker scoped only to this case.

Updated the existing stalled-manuscript test fixture (it hard-coded the old global ceiling) and rewrote the real-engine end-to-end test to call advance_build repeatedly, as production now does, asserting progress never regresses below 30%. Added a new test giving every chapter a real, measurable delay, proving no single advance_build call ever waits for more than about one chapter's worth of it -- the literal, timed reproduction of the worker-timeout risk this release closes.

Followed the required proof order: targeted tests -> 195 + 176 broader manuscript/ebook tests -> Fast Gate (160 passed, 698 subtests) -> Full Gate (2870 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped, 0 paid API calls) -- never running the Full Gate first.

Committed as c9ab112 and pushed to origin/main. Could not perform the live re-test myself, and could not confirm the actual Render timeout/Start Command -- both remain open for the owner, now for a fourth consecutive fix in this sprint.

completed_log.date: 2026-09-13/14 (ebook generator recovery sprint, part 3 -- manuscript QA/correction)
items: The provider-routing fix (v1.7.8) held on the next live build: 'Container Gardening Step by Step' advanced past chapter generation for the first time in this sprint, then failed at manuscript QA/approval with a new, unrelated error.
Live traceback attempt 1: 'Resolve structural/content findings before approving the manuscript.' Attempt 2 (same build, retried): 'Cannot approve an empty manuscript.'

Read-only trace first, per the sprint's requirement: confirmed via services/ebook_project_workspace.py::approve_stage's own check order that attempt 1's content was genuinely non-empty (the empty check runs before the needs-correction check), so the structural/content findings were real, not a false empty-content path.

Found the single root cause behind both distinct error messages: services/ebook_build_orchestrator.py::advance_build's exception handler persisted the data snapshot captured BEFORE the stage runner ran, on every failure -- silently discarding whatever the runner's own persist_progress callback had already saved (accepted chapters) and the runner's own final result (the assembled manuscript, QA findings, stage status), none of which the failure path ever used.

Separately found that _run_manuscript never invoked services.ebook_project_workspace.execute_correct_manuscript -- an existing, fully-built manuscript-correction system (the same one a human uses via 'Request Correction') -- and instead called approve_stage() directly, which is guaranteed to raise whenever the stage needs correction.

Implemented three coordinated, minimal fixes: (1) _run_manuscript now runs the existing correction pass automatically once before approving, and skips straight to correction on a resumed attempt that already has a preserved NEEDS_CORRECTION draft, never re-triggering generation over it; (2) _run_manuscript persists an explicit checkpoint after generation and after correction, before approve_stage runs; (3) advance_build's exception handler re-reads the database before recording a failure, so a failure can only add information, never erase already-saved progress. Added the same persist_progress support to execute_correct_manuscript that execute_generate_manuscript already had.
No second manuscript-correction system was built -- the existing one is now actually reachable from the automatic build, exactly as required.

Added tests/test_ebook_manuscript_correction_recovery.py (6 tests, zero paid calls): the centerpiece drives the Factory's own real 10-chapter acceptance-project fixture through real generation, correction and approval with only the chapter-writer replaced, proving 9 already-good chapters are never regenerated (called exactly once each) while the one genuinely flawed chapter is repaired automatically and the build advances from 30% to 40%; five more tests pin content preservation, correct resume-to-correction routing, and a genuine empty-manuscript failure staying clear and honest.

Followed the required proof order: targeted tests -> 189 + 188 broader manuscript/ebook tests -> Fast Gate (160 passed, 698 subtests) -> Full Gate (2869 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped, 0 paid API calls) -- never running the Full Gate first.
Committed as ca33aa0 and pushed to origin/main. Could not perform the live re-test myself -- this remains the one open item, now for the third consecutive fix in this sprint.

items: The owner ran a NEW live ebook build after the v1.7.7 fix deployed and got the identical failure -- proving that fix's RENDER-environment-variable check did not actually engage in the real deployed runtime. The owner explicitly stopped this session from assuming success just because tests passed, and required proof from a fresh live traceback before any further change.

New live traceback confirmed: services.ai_providers.ProviderUnavailable: Local engine unreachable at http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/chat: Connection refused -- same generate_one_chapter call chain, meaning select_provider() still chose LocalAIProvider in production despite v1.7.7's RENDER check.

Traced why: v1.7.7's _running_on_render() rested on an unverified assumption (that the hosting platform auto-injects a RENDER variable) that the live evidence disproved for this deployment. Ruled out other candidates directly: no other call path bypasses routes_local(); provider selection is not cached ahead of the policy check; .env does not define RENDER, so dotenv override was not the mechanism for that specific variable.

Rather than attempt a third detection method, changed the actual default: services/ai_providers.py's DEFAULT_POLICY is now POLICY_PREMIUM (cloud), not POLICY_LOCAL_FIRST. Local chapter generation is opt-in ONLY -- FACTORY_AI_POLICY must be explicitly 'local_first' or 'local_only' -- so a missing, wrong, or not-carried-forward setting means cloud, on any hosting platform, without needing to recognize it. Removed the RENDER-detection code from v1.7.7 entirely.

Preserved local Windows Ollama support: added the one explicit opt-in line to the owner's own .env (gitignored, not committed) and documented the same contract in .env.example with an explicit warning never to set it on a hosted deployment.

Updated tests/test_ai_providers.py's baseline fixture to the new opt-in contract and added the core production-safety test proving a missing policy defaults to premium, never local. Rewrote tests/test_ai_provider_render_safety.py (10 tests) for the corrected mechanism.

While rewriting these tests, found and fixed a real test-infrastructure bug of the exact same shape as the production incident: ai_client.py's own load_dotenv(override=True) fired mid-test via a lazy first import, silently re-injecting .env's FACTORY_AI_POLICY after the test's own cleanup -- fixed by importing ai_client at module level.
